title: Matrix Calculus & Geometry
description: Study gradients of quadratic forms, jacobians and vector transformations, hessians and local curvature, and singular values and conditioning. Each lesson includes a worked example and an applied practice task.

lessons.title: Gradients of quadratic forms
lessons.description: Compute the gradient at x = (2,1) and verify one component with a finite difference.
lessons.conceptOverview: For a scalar quadratic f(x) = x transpose A x, the gradient is (A + A transpose)x. If A is symmetric this becomes 2Ax. State vector shapes explicitly to avoid confusing scalar derivatives with matrix products.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: For a scalar quadratic f(x) = x transpose A x, the gradient is (A + A transpose)x. If A is symmetric this becomes 2Ax. State vector shapes explicitly to avoid confusing scalar derivatives with matrix products.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For A equal to the diagonal matrix with entries 2 and 3 and x = (1,2), the gradient is (4,12).

sections.title: Practice & verification
sections.content: Compute the gradient at x = (2,1) and verify one component with a finite difference. Write down your reasoning and check it against the concept before continuing.

commonMistakes: The gradient of every quadratic is Ax without any factor or symmetry condition.

lessons.title: Jacobians and vector transformations
lessons.description: Trace the dimensions of an upstream two-element gradient propagated back to the three inputs.
lessons.conceptOverview: A Jacobian records the partial derivatives of each output with respect to each input. For y = Wx, the Jacobian with respect to x is W; reverse-mode propagation multiplies an upstream gradient by W transpose.
lessons.whyItMatters: Reverse-mode gradient propagation respects the transpose and shape contract.
lessons.engineerDeepDive: A Jacobian records the partial derivatives of each output with respect to each input. For y = Wx, the Jacobian with respect to x is W; reverse-mode propagation multiplies an upstream gradient by W transpose.

sections.title: Concept

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A map from three inputs to two outputs has a 2 by 3 Jacobian.

sections.title: Practice & verification
sections.content: Trace the dimensions of an upstream two-element gradient propagated back to the three inputs. Write down your reasoning and check it against the concept before continuing.

keyTakeaways: Reverse-mode gradient propagation respects the transpose and shape contract.
commonMistakes: The input gradient has the same dimension as the output regardless of W.

lessons.title: Hessians and local curvature
lessons.description: Compute the Hessian and explain why the origin is not a minimum.
lessons.conceptOverview: The Hessian contains second derivatives and describes local curvature for sufficiently smooth functions. Positive definiteness implies a strict local minimum at a stationary point; an indefinite Hessian indicates a saddle.
lessons.whyItMatters: Zero gradient alone does not establish a minimum.
lessons.engineerDeepDive: The Hessian contains second derivatives and describes local curvature for sufficiently smooth functions. Positive definiteness implies a strict local minimum at a stationary point; an indefinite Hessian indicates a saddle.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: The Hessian contains second derivatives and describes local curvature for sufficiently smooth functions. Positive definiteness implies a strict local minimum at a stationary point; an indefinite Hessian indicates a saddle.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For f(x,y) = x squared minus y squared, the origin is stationary but curvature has opposite signs along the axes.

sections.title: Practice & verification
sections.content: Compute the Hessian and explain why the origin is not a minimum. Write down your reasoning and check it against the concept before continuing.

keyTakeaways: Zero gradient alone does not establish a minimum.
commonMistakes: Every stationary point is a local minimum.

lessons.title: Singular values and conditioning
lessons.description: Perturb the second measurement and calculate the resulting solution difference.
lessons.conceptOverview: Singular values describe how a linear map stretches directions. A large ratio between largest and smallest nonzero singular values signals sensitivity in inversion or least squares; rank deficiency adds non-uniqueness.
lessons.whyItMatters: Ill-conditioned systems can amplify measurement errors.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Singular values describe how a linear map stretches directions. A large ratio between largest and smallest nonzero singular values signals sensitivity in inversion or least squares; rank deficiency adds non-uniqueness.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A diagonal system has entries 1 and 0.000001, so small noise in the second measurement can create a large solution change.

sections.title: Practice & verification
sections.content: Perturb the second measurement and calculate the resulting solution difference. Write down your reasoning and check it against the concept before continuing.

keyTakeaways: Ill-conditioned systems can amplify measurement errors.
commonMistakes: Small input errors always produce equally small inverse-solution errors.
